description:
Lynda.com Is Now LinkedIn Learning: Find the Right Course and Build a Practice Project

If you followed an old Lynda.com bookmark, start your search on LinkedIn Learning. LinkedIn completed the transition from Lynda.com in 2021. An old bookmark can still give you the name of an instructor or a useful topic, but the current catalog is where you should check course availability, lesson contents, and how to sign in. If you need a completion record from an old account, contact the organization that provided access or use the current LinkedIn Learning support channel. Have the old course title and the approximate completion date ready.

It is easy to spend longer comparing classes than practicing the skill you wanted to learn. A better starting point is a small job you expect to do again. In the example throughout this guide, a shop assistant wants to build a spreadsheet that tracks stock counts. The goal is a file a colleague can open and use at the end of each week. The same approach works for a first video edit, a presentation, or an introductory coding project. Choose an outcome, find the lesson that helps you reach it, then test yourself on an example of your own.

Decide what you want to do after the lesson

Write down a task in language you would use with a coworker. “I want to get better at spreadsheets” is hard to test. “I want to record a weekly count and flag items below their reorder level” gives you two actions to practice and a visible result. The shop assistant can check whether a line becomes highlighted when its count falls below the threshold. A colleague can also try adding a new item and see whether the same rule applies to it.

Think about where the skill will be used. A spreadsheet built for one person on a laptop may need different instructions from a sheet shared by staff on several devices. Find out which applications the team already uses, whether files are stored locally or online, and how people identify items. If the shop already uses product codes, use a few fictional codes in the exercise. If different items are measured in boxes and pieces, give the count and threshold consistent units for each row.

Make your first version small. The tracker could begin with six items and three actions. Enter a count, display a reorder flag, and filter the list to see which items need attention. Leave purchasing integrations and supplier reports for another exercise. When the assistant can complete the smaller task without following a video step by step, there is a reliable base for adding features.

Find your access route before planning a course

Start with the organization you expect to use. An employer might provide a learning portal, a college might have a student sign-in page, and a library might publish a separate route for eligible members. Follow the instructions supplied by that organization and confirm that the course is visible when signed in through it. Access through one route does not establish that another route includes the same catalog, downloads, or account features. A learner comparing individual access should check the current offer from LinkedIn Learning.

If you used Lynda.com through a past employer or school, keep that context when asking about an old record. Share the old email address only through an appropriate support channel. A current subscription and a historic completion record are separate questions. You can use a course today without recovering the previous record, and you can ask about historic learning without assuming a new subscription restores it. Ask what evidence is available before creating a duplicate profile or paying for access simply to retrieve a certificate.

If you landed on a third-party listing, confirm the exact current product, the sign-in route, and the term before relying on it. The legacy name alone does not identify the catalog or the kind of account you will receive. If work or school needs to recognize the training, ask that organization which route it accepts. Keep receipts and account details in a secure place you control, and make sure you can retain the work you create even if your catalog access changes.

Search the catalog by task, application, and version

Start with the feature you need to learn. Try searches such as spreadsheet tables, filtering rows, conditional formatting, or basic inventory tracking. Compare the syllabus with the small project you defined. If you already know how to create a workbook and enter rows, you might begin with a short lesson on tables. If you have never written a comparison formula, choose a foundation lesson that explains operators and cell references before taking on formatting rules.

Check which version or application the instructor uses. A demonstration for desktop Excel may show a different path from the web version. A formula may still work while the menus look unfamiliar. If the course uses a feature your team cannot access, decide whether it teaches a concept you can transfer or whether you need a closer match. Read the description and preview a lesson that performs a recognizable task. Look for the actual steps, not just a visually polished introduction.

Save one main course and a short fallback. A fallback might be a lesson that explains a single feature more slowly. Write down where each resource fits. For the inventory tracker, a general table course may explain sorting and structured ranges. A separate conditional formatting lesson may help the assistant highlight a low count. The courses can have different instructors while supporting the same result. Keeping the list short leaves more time to work in the spreadsheet.

Use the preview and syllabus to judge the teaching

Choose a preview section where the instructor demonstrates something. Listen for why the instructor chooses a feature and how they check whether it worked. If the lesson creates a filter, watch whether it explains how to clear the filter and restore every row. Those small details help when a learner has to use the feature without the demonstration. A preview can also tell you whether the pacing leaves enough time to follow the screen.

Look at the order of the lessons. A course might begin with file setup and spend several modules on topics unrelated to your task. You can still use the relevant chapters if you understand the prerequisites. Read the titles before committing to the whole course. If a beginner lesson assumes comfort with named ranges or chart settings, find out early. A short practice session is easier to finish when it introduces only one unfamiliar idea at a time.

Check whether the course supplies exercise files if you want to follow the instructor closely. LinkedIn Learning has help documentation for exercise files. The course page and your access route can tell you what is available for the lesson you choose. A provided example is useful for reproducing the instructor's steps. After that, make your own small dataset with different values to see whether you understood the feature. You may discover that your rule only worked on the rows or units used in the recording.

Set up a spreadsheet you can finish in one sitting

Create a workbook with a place for the data and another for short instructions. On the data sheet, use columns for item code, item name, unit, current count, reorder level, and status. Add six fictional products. Include a row whose count is below the threshold, one that equals it, and one that is above it. This gives you cases to check without importing records from the shop's live stock system.

Write the rule on the instructions sheet before building a formula. For this demonstration, the shop wants to reorder when the current count is lower than the reorder level. If the count equals the threshold, it will appear as adequate. A real team might use a rule that includes equality. Ask the person who handles purchasing which rule belongs in production. What matters in the exercise is that you can write the intended rule and test it against numbers chosen for that purpose.

Add a date field or a simple way to identify the count period. Decide whether the sheet represents one week at a time or keeps a history. A first workbook can record one week and let staff save a fresh copy for the next count. If the team needs to compare stock over time, that can become a second project. Give the file a recognizable name and keep an untouched copy so you can start again if a test changes several rows.

Follow the demonstration and repeat it with your own data

Watch the lesson once to see the completed result. Then set up your own data and repeat the core steps. For the stock tracker, format the rows as a table if your application supports that workflow. Try sorting by item name and then by current count. Check that the product code and quantity move together. If you find yourself sorting one column independently, undo the change and review how the instructor selects a range or applies the table command.

Next, add a status formula that checks the two numbers on the same row. A simple example using regular Excel cell references is =IF(D2<E2,"Reorder","OK"), assuming the current count is in column D and the reorder level is in E. Test the formula with your three expected cases. Change a count while you watch the status. If the output stays the same when it should change, inspect the referenced cells before trying another formula. Some spreadsheet applications or locale settings use a different argument separator, so match the syntax shown in your own setup.

Decide what should happen when a field is blank. A missing stock count should not be mistaken for a confirmed count of zero. You can handle that early by leaving the status blank until both inputs are present. If you have only learned the basic comparison so far, document that limitation and turn the blank-field rule into a follow-up exercise. This is better practice than copying a complicated formula without understanding when it produces an answer. Keep the test values beside your notes so you can repeat the same checks later.

Design the file for the colleague who will use it

Ask a colleague to test a clean copy with a fictional count. Give them only the instructions sheet and tell them the expected task. Observe which cells they edit first. If they type into the status column, distinguish inputs from computed results with headings and a short note. If they enter quantities in boxes where the threshold is shown in individual pieces, put the unit beside each numeric field. The instructions should resolve the issue where the person makes the choice.

Use clear visual cues. A red fill can draw attention to items that need review, but the status text should convey the same information. Try the sheet with the window narrowed and check whether the columns you need remain easy to identify. If staff sort or filter results, give them a short note about how to return to the full list. Save an example of the expected result so that a new user can compare their first copy with it.

Write two or three handoff lines. Explain who sets the reorder threshold, how the date is recorded, and where completed copies belong. Add one sentence about what to do if a product code is missing or duplicated. A workbook grows harder to maintain when different people invent their own answers to these questions. The first draft need only cover the common actions. Record any exceptions you discover as you observe the shop using it.

Build a simple review around what you can do independently

Close the course and recreate the tracker with different item names. Try to recall the order of the steps before consulting your notes. If you remember the formula but cannot explain which row it refers to, revisit the lesson on cell references. If you can explain the rule but forget where the menu is, spend a few minutes finding the command. Those are different gaps and deserve different practice. Write down the one that caused you to pause.

Give yourself a new constraint. For example, add two items while the list is filtered, then clear the filter and verify that the items appear in the full list. Or change a threshold after a reviewer has already entered the count and check that the status updates. A small variation shows whether you can adapt the method. Keep it realistic. Adding a separate accounting system is a different project, while checking how the table handles a new item is a useful extension of the original lesson.

Save your finished workbook with a short explanation of the test cases and what the file currently supports. If it contains fictional data, label it that way. A supervisor reviewing it can then see how the result relates to the learning objective. If you want to include a sample in a public portfolio, use data you created or have permission to share. Keep internal inventory and supplier details out of the demonstration. The same project can show a real skill without exposing the business records you work with.

Plan study time around small deliverables

Schedule a first session to select a course and reproduce one example. Use a second session to build the six-row tracker. Use the third to test boundary cases and write instructions. Set a realistic time limit for each session and leave a note for the next one. If you only have twenty minutes, you can still test changing a count and see whether the status behaves as expected. A clear next action helps you resume without watching the earlier lessons again.

When several courses cover related material, spend more time practicing than collecting recommendations. An advanced course may make sense after you uncover a concrete need, such as summarizing weekly results in a chart. A task you can explain in one or two sentences gives you a better search query. It also tells you which chapters you can save for later. For the shop, a monthly trend chart becomes useful once people are reliably saving comparable weekly counts.

Record the version of the software and the date you practiced. If the application changes, you can often reuse the underlying logic while checking the new menu paths. Write a note when an instruction only works on desktop or when a shared workbook behaves differently. Your notes should help you reproduce the outcome without guessing which environment the recording showed. Keep the working file and its instructions together so a manager can review both during a training handoff.

Understand certificates and check any external requirement

LinkedIn Learning explains which courses and learning paths can award a Certificate of Completion. Check the details for the specific course. If an employer, school, or professional body requires evidence of training, ask what it accepts before starting. A course completion record and a professional certification may satisfy different requirements. Find out whether you need a specific evaluation, a signed verification, or a project reviewed by someone in your organization.

For everyday professional development, pair the completion record with a clear example of what you learned. For this project, you could show a sample workbook and explain the rule that flags a count for review. Point out one problem you found in testing and how you corrected it. If you adapted the workbook for the web edition of your application, show what changed. A reviewer can assess your judgment from the project and see how the course contributed.

Check your access before promising that a colleague can download the same materials. A link to a course may be useful even when the other person needs their own approved access route. Share your original instructions and test file when permitted. If the instructor supplied exercise files, check their terms before redistributing them. Give the colleague a clear task to try, so they can use your notes even if their version of the software looks a little different.

Choose the next lesson based on the first review

At the end of the practice sessions, pick one improvement that fits the way your team works. If coworkers need a quick view of the items below their threshold, learn how to build a filtered summary. If they mainly struggle with typing consistent product codes, practice data validation. Keep a copy of the first workbook so you can compare the change with the simpler version. Ask the same colleague to repeat the original task before calling the revision an improvement. Write down what they completed faster and where they still needed help. Use that observation to choose your next lesson.

Frequently asked questions

What happened to Lynda.com?

LinkedIn completed the transition from Lynda.com to LinkedIn Learning in 2021. Use the current catalog to check courses and access. If you are looking for an old record, start with the institution or account route that supplied the original access.

Can I find the exact course from an old bookmark?

Search the current catalog by course title, instructor, and the skill you need. If you cannot locate the original, read the syllabus of a current course that covers the same task. Verify the application version through its description or preview.

Do I need to finish a whole course before starting a project?

Begin practicing when you have enough instruction to complete a small task. You can return to more lessons as you meet a specific problem. If your employer requires full course completion, track that separately and check the applicable rules.

What makes a good practice project?

Choose a job with an observable result and at least one condition you can test. A stock tracker should respond when a count crosses a threshold. A presentation should be readable and explain one decision. Save your result and describe how you checked it.
